hero.title: Biodiversity Hotspots In India
hero.description: Biodiversity hotspots are biogeographic regions characterized by exceptional levels of plant endemism and serious levels of habitat loss. For Allahabad High Court RO/ARO and UPPSC examinations, questions frequently test the exact number of global and Indian hotspots, endemic species, and specific geographical boundaries.

timeline.title: Evolution of Biodiversity Hotspots Concept
timeline.description: Chronological milestones tracing the formulation and expansion of the Biodiversity Hotspots framework.

cards.details: British ecologist Norman Myers coined the term 'Biodiversity Hotspot' to identify priority regions for conservation.
Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers' hotspots and directed a re-evaluation to include strict quantitative criteria.
CI published an updated global analysis, expanding the list to 25 terrestrial hotspots worldwide, including the Western Ghats and Eastern Himalayas in India.
CI added new regions, raising the global count to 34 hotspots. Sundaland and Indo-Burma were officially added, directly impacting Indian territorial conservation scopes.
The total global count stands at 36 hotspots, with India hosting parts of 4 major biodiversity hotspots.

items.question: How many biodiversity hotspots are recognized globally as of current updates?
Which Indian island group represents a part of the Sundaland biodiversity hotspot?
What is the minimum percentage of primary vegetation loss required for a region to qualify as a hotspot?
items.answer: At least 70% loss of its original habitat.

traps.title: Common Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Andaman vs. Nicobar in Sundaland: Aspirants often assume the entire Andaman and Nicobar archipelago is part of Sundaland. Only the Nicobar Islands group is included in the Sundaland hotspot, while Andaman Islands are biogeographically distinct.
Total Hotspots Count Confusion: Do not confuse the original 25 hotspots (from the year 2000) or 34 hotspots (2005) with the current established count of 36 global hotspots.

deepDive.title: Biodiversity Hotspots In India Core Study Notes
deepDive.description: Biodiversity hotspots are biogeographic regions characterized by exceptional levels of plant endemism and serious levels of habitat loss. For Allahabad High Court RO/ARO and UPPSC examinations, questions frequently test the exact number of global and Indian hotspots, endemic species, and specific geographical boundaries.

sections.title: Criteria and Definition of Hotspots
sections.content:
Understanding the stringent ecological benchmarks established by Conservation International to classify a region as a biodiversity hotspot.

  • Endemism Requirement: A region must contain at least 1,500 species of vascular plants (> 0.5% of the world's total) as endemics, meaning they are found nowhere else on Earth.
  • Habitat Loss Criterion: The region must have lost at least 70% of its original primary vegetation, indicating extreme anthropogenic threat and vulnerability.
  • Global Significance: Despite covering less than 2.5% of Earth's land surface, hotspots support over 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile, and amphibian species.
  • Role of Conservation International: Conservation International (CI) acts as the primary governing scientific body monitoring, updating, and funding global hotspot designations.

sections.title: The Four Biodiversity Hotspots in India
sections.content:
India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries globally, harbouring parts of four distinct biodiversity hotspots.

  • 1. Western Ghats (Sahyadri): Stretches along the western coast of peninsular India across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Noted for high endemism in amphibians, reptiles, and tropical evergreen flora.
  • 2. Eastern Himalayas: Encompasses Bhutan, north-east India, and southern, central China. Extremely rich in alpine flora, orchids, and high-altitude fauna like the Red Panda and Snow Leopard.
  • 3. Indo-Burma Region: Spans across north-eastern India (south of Brahmaputra river), Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia. Famous for freshwater turtle diversity and large mammal endemism.
  • 4. Sundaland: Includes Southeast Asian islands such as Sumatra, Borneo, Java, and the Nicobar Islands group of India. Celebrated for rich marine ecosystems and iconic species like the Orangutan.

sections.title: Key Endemic Species and Ecological Threats
sections.content:
Exam questions frequently target the unique flora and fauna restricted strictly to these designated Indian zones.

  • Lion-tailed Macaque (Macaca silenus): Endemic to the evergreen forests of the Western Ghats; listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, highly sensitive to forest fragmentation.
  • Nilgiri Tahr (Nilgiritragus hylocrius): State animal of Tamil Nadu, found exclusively in the high-altitude montane grasslands (Sholas) of the southern Western Ghats.
  • Red Panda (Ailurus fulgens): Inhabits the temperate forests of the Eastern Himalayas; feeds heavily on bamboo and faces threats from poaching and habitat loss.
  • Major Anthropogenic Pressures: Deforestation for tea/coffee plantations, illegal mining, infrastructure expansion (roads/railways through eco-sensitive zones), and climate shift.
